title: Maintain optimal environmental conditions for floristry arrangements

lessons.title: What flowers need to last
lessons.html:
What flowers need to last

Cut flowers and foliage are still alive after they are cut. They keep breathing and losing water, but they can no longer take water from roots. A florist's job is to slow down ageing so arrangements stay fresh for the customer as long as possible. The right environment can make the difference between flowers that last two days and flowers that last a week or more.

Things that shorten vase life

  • Heat: warm air makes flowers breathe faster and use up their food. They open and die quickly.
  • Dry air and wind: flowers lose water through petals and leaves and wilt.
  • Direct sun: heats the flowers and the water.
  • Dirty water: bacteria grow and block the stems so water cannot get up.
  • Ethylene gas: a natural gas given off by ripening fruit, dying flowers, and car fumes. It makes many flowers, such as carnations, drop petals or wilt early.
  • Rough handling: bruised petals rot.

The best conditions

FactorGood practice
TemperatureCool. Store in a cool room or flower fridge set as your shop instructs. Keep tropical flowers like anthuriums out of very cold air, as they get cold damage.
HumidityMoist air. A cool room keeps humidity high. Misting helps some foliage.
LightBright, indirect light in the shop. No direct sun.
AirNo strong draughts from fans, doors or air conditioners.
WaterClean buckets and vases, fresh water, flower food.

Always keep fruit and vegetables out of the flower cool room. A box of bananas can damage a whole cool room of flowers.

lessons.title: Daily care of arrangements and storage areas
lessons.html:
Daily care

In the cool room

  • Check the thermometer every morning and afternoon. Write the reading in the log.
  • Report to your supervisor if the temperature is wrong or the unit makes strange noises.
  • Keep the door closed. Do not leave it open while you carry stock in and out.
  • Do not overcrowd buckets. Air must move around the flowers.
  • Keep the floor and shelves clean. Remove dropped leaves and petals every day; they rot and give off ethylene.

Caring for arrangements

  1. Check the water level every day. Top up with fresh water and flower food. Floral foam must never dry out; once dry, it does not soak up water well again.
  2. Remove wilted or damaged flowers and leaves.
  3. Mist foliage if the flower type allows. Do not mist flowers that spot or rot when wet.
  4. Move displays away from sunny windows, heaters and air conditioner vents.
  5. In the shop window on hot days, rotate displays to the cool room for part of the day.

Buckets and vases

  • Wash buckets and vases with detergent and a little household bleach or the sanitiser your shop uses, then rinse well.
  • Change water in stock buckets regularly, recutting stems each time.
  • Never put fresh flowers in a dirty bucket.

Delivering arrangements

  • Keep the delivery vehicle cool. Do not leave arrangements in a parked car in the sun.
  • Secure arrangements so they do not fall over.
  • Give the customer care advice: keep cool, out of sun and away from fruit, top up water.

Safety

Cleaning chemicals must be used as the label says, with gloves. Never mix bleach with other cleaners. Wipe up water spills at once; wet floors in a flower shop are slippery.

Key points

  • Keep flowers cool, humid, out of direct sun and away from draughts.
  • Keep fruit and rotting plant material away; they give off ethylene.
  • Check and log cool room temperature daily.
  • Top up water and flower food and never let foam dry out.
  • Use clean buckets and vases every time.
